fetched_contents.text: Near‐infrared spectroscopy enables quality selection in wheat breeding - Walker - 2023 - Cereal Chemistry Abstract Background and Objectives Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and small-scale testing are used to evaluate wheat germplasm is a cost-effective strategy to reduce thousands of wheat lines to hundreds and then to tens of lines. Identification of high-quality germplasm among thousands of lines is dependent on the accuracy of the tests that are used and how well these data correlate with the large-scale tests that are used to confirm the end-use quality before commercial release of a new wheat variety. In this study, NIR-based testing was investigated to determine the effectiveness of this high-throughput, nondestructive technology. Findings To demonstrate the effectiveness of NIRS and small-scale testing as a selection strategy, interpretive population statistics evaluating three consecutive generations (F4, F5, and F6) from a wheat breeding program were compared. The F4 (early stage) generation (2019) was predicted for milling yield with a proportion of 13.9% of lines above 74% (w/w) milling yield. From those lines that progressed to F5 (mid-generation in 2020), the proportion increased to 26.2% of lines above 74% (w/w) milling yield. Selected lines from F5 were progressed to F6 (advanced generation in 2021), where 62.4% of lines were above 74% (w/w) milling yield. Conclusions Each time the set progressed through the selection strategy, the portion of lines above 74% (w/w) milling yield increased. Significance and Novelty This study demonstrates the value and efficiency of high-throughput selection strategies using nondestructive NIRS at the F4 (early-stage generation) stage and small-scale testing at the F5 stage of a wheat breeding program. 1 INTRODUCTION Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is the preferred method to quantify the composition of grains and seeds as minimal sample processing is required and samples can be rapidly measured on a whole-grain basis. NIRS is an accepted standard method and is used to routinely determine the percentage protein (AACC-39-25-01) and hardness (AACC-39-70-02) of wheat (AACC, 2020; Williams & Norris, 2001). The accuracy of NIRS in the application of grain classification is that in standard methodologies for protein concentration, the calibration statistics observed are recommended to be less than ≤0.25 for the standard error (SECV%) and greater than ≥0.98 for the correlation coefficient (Williams & Sobering, 1993). The application of high-throughput platforms in plant breeding can enable rapid analysis of small quantities of grain and is suitable for selection of germplasm in early generations when the grain is limited (Assadzadeh et al., 2020; Black & Panozzo, 2002; Hayes et al., 2017). Historically, small-scale testing has been used to select germplasm in the early generations, where 20–50 g of grain can be destructively assessed for milling and flour quality (O'Brien et al., 1989), using small-scale flour milling tests, sedimentation tests such as the sodium dodecyl sulfate sedimentation test, solvent retention capacity, swelling power, and small-scale mixers (Békés et al., 2001; Fischer et al., 1989; O'Brien & Ronalds, 1986; Seabourn et al., 2012). These tests have been developed to identify lines of commercial significance selected for improved milling yield and to identify dough rheology traits important in the baking or noodle processing industries. Small-scale tests are widely accepted for early-generation selection purposes in wheat breeding but are labor intensive, testing between 30 and 100 samples a day, and are destructive to the grain (Békés et al., 2001; Black & Panozzo, 1999; Black et al., 2000). Using nondestructive technologies such as NIRS can enable breeding programs to predict quality traits, as NIRS testing is cost-effective, rapid, and high throughput, measures multiple traits, and after testing, the grain can then be utilized as a seed source in field trials to advance germplasm into the next generation (Assadzadeh et al., 2020; Black & Panozzo, 1999, 2004; Delwiche & Graybosch, 2003; Hayes et al., 2017; Walker & Panozzo, 2014). Development of applications based on NIRS analysis in early generations of a wheat breeding program can be problematic, particularly as milling, dough rheology, and end-product quality traits in testing the quality require large quantities of grain, approximately 2–5 kg (Azizinia et al., 2023). Processing wheat to flour and an end-product, such as bread or noodles, involves multiple steps, such as milling to flour, mixing a dough, sheeting for noodles, or fermentation and baking. Therefore, prediction of the % milling yield or % water absorption on whole-grain samples using spectral signatures is complex. Factors that influence the accuracy of the NIRS calibration include the need for consistent laboratory data with low error and NIRS instrumentation of appropriate sensitivity to ensure the maximum chance of identifying precursors within the spectra associated with the trait of interest (Walker & Panozzo, 2014). Complex processing traits require rigorous validation with reference methods to ensure that calibrations can be reliably applied to predict key phenotypic quality traits in large and diverse breeding populations. As germplasm progresses through the breeding cycle, larger quantities of grain become available for destructive testing. Therefore, in the latter stages, when grain can be destructively tested, full reference testing is undertaken to ensure that lines that progress through the breeding program meet market needs. fetched_contents.text: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Analysis of the Phytic Acid Content in Fuzzy Cottonseed Based on Machine Learning Algorithms Abstract Cottonseed is rich in oil and protein. However, its antinutritional factor content, of phytic acid (PA), has limited its utilization. Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, combined with chemometrics, is an efficient and eco-friendly analytical technique for crop quality analysis. Despite its potential, there are currently no established NIR models for measuring the PA content in fuzzy cottonseeds. In this research, a total of 456 samples of fuzzy cottonseed were used as the experimental materials. Spectral pre-treatments, including first derivative (1D) and standard normal variable transformation (SNV), were applied, and the linear partial least squares (PLS), nonlinear support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF) methods were utilized to develop accurate calibration models for predicting the content of PA in fuzzy cottonseed. The results showed that the spectral pre-treatment significantly improved the prediction performance of the models, with the RF model exhibiting the best prediction performance. The RF model had a coefficient of determination in prediction (R2p) of 0.9114, and its residual predictive deviation (RPD) was 3.9828, which indicates its high accuracy in measuring the PA content in fuzzy cottonseed. Additionally, this method avoids the costly and time-consuming delinting and crushing of cottonseeds, making it an economical and environmentally friendly alternative. Keywords: near-infrared spectroscopy, fuzzy cottonseed, phytic acid, models 1. Introduction Cottonseed is a widely available by-product of cotton processing with high yield potential [1]. Cottonseed contains an array of essential nutrients, such as proteins, oils, fatty acids, and amino acids, making it a valuable raw material for various industrial applications [2]. Through processing, cottonseed can yield valuable products, including cottonseed oil, cottonseed protein, and other derivatives [3]. Cottonseed oil contains essential fatty acids such as linoleic acid and vitamin E. It has good effects in reducing blood cholesterol and antioxidation, making it a high-quality edible oil. It is also one of the main sources of vegetable oil for residents in cotton-producing areas in China. And due to its good stability and crispness, cottonseed oil can be used to make frying oil, shortening, and margarine, and it is used as a substitute for hydrogenated vegetable oil, containing trans fatty acids, in multiple countries. In the industrial sector, cottonseed oil serves as starting material for the synthesis of stearic acid, soft fatty acids, glycerol, and malonic acid, among others [4,5]. Cottonseed is not only a high-quality oil source but also a great protein resource. Many countries have conducted early research on the application of cottonseed protein in food and have developed several edible products. For example, defatted cottonseed protein powder has been added to dried pancakes, donuts, and chocolate candies, and cottonseed protein powder has been widely used as a food additive and flour mixture in cooking [6]. Cottonseed soup is considered a delicacy on the cooking table in some countries on the Asian continent, such as India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, and the African continent [7]. In addition, the residue of cottonseed after oil extraction, known as cottonseed meal, is used as a fertilizer or a protein source in ruminant animal nutrition. With the research and development of detoxification techniques for cottonseed meal, it has been widely utilized in poultry and monogastric animal feeding, serving as a protein source in feed for chickens, ducks, geese, pigs, and aquaculture [8]. In summary, cottonseed is a by-product with immense potential in various industries, including the food and industrial sectors. However, cotton itself carries an anti-nutritional factor, phytic acid (PA) [9]. PA is the primary phosphorus (P) storage compound in seeds [10]. The molecular formula of PA is C6H18O24P6, and it consists of six phosphate groups and an inositol ring. PA is a valuable raw material used in various industries, including the food, medicine, polymer, metal processing, and fuel industries. However, monogastric animals (such as poultry, swine, and fish) cannot digest phytic acid due to the limited presence or absence of phytase activity in their digestive tract. As a result, these animals release a significant amount of phosphorus into the environment, leading to water pollution through eutrophication [11,12,13]. Furthermore, PA is considered to inhibit the uptake of several essential minerals (especially Fe and Zn), and macro-nutrients like protein, starch, and lipids [14,15]. “Low PA” content as a trait of seeds can provide many potential benefits [13]. Researchers have devoted themselves to reducing their PA content, including using genetic improvements, as well as various pre-treatment methods, such as fermentation, soaking, germination, and the enzymatic treatment of grains with phytase. The rapid and accurate determination of the PA content in a large number of samples is often needed [16]. Currently, the conventional method of high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is the most commonly used technique for measuring PA content [17]. Unfortunately, this method is time-consuming and costly. Furthermore, when preparing cottonseed samples for analysis using this method, the fuzzy cottonseed needs to be delinted with concentrated sulfuric acid, which damages part of the sample, increasing the costs. The discharge of concentrated sulfuric acid waste liquor after depilation also causes the corrosion of pipelines, soil acidification, and other environmental problems. Rapid and non-destructive near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can effectively solve the above problems. fetched_contents.text: The influence of phytate-bound-phosphorus on the near infrared spectra of wheat grains Abstract Near infrared (NIR) spectroscopy has been used to determine total phosphorus (total-P), phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus concentrations in grains and animal feeds. However, since more than 50% of the total-P in grains of most cultivated cereals occurs as phytate (myo-inositolhexakisphosphate), there is a strong linear correlation between total-P and phytate-bound-P. If near infrared spectroscopy is used to analyse cereal products simultaneously for both total-P and for phytate-bound-P there is a risk that the intercorrelation effects will be dominant in models for each. This paper presents NIR spectra of whole wheat grains from progeny of a normal and a low phytate parent genotype. For these progeny there was a weak correlation between the phytate-bound-P and total-P concentrations (r = 0.5) and no correlation with grain protein (r = 0.1). The spectra of grains with lower phytate-bound-P differed at wavelengths that aligned mainly with O-H, C-H and P-OH bonds and included 7124 cm−1 (1404 nm), 5882 cm−1 (1701 nm) and 5245 cm−1 (1907 nm). Loading weights for partial least squares regression models indicated that models for both total-P and phytate-bound-P utilized essentially the same wavelengths. This supports the hypothesis that NIR calibrations for total-P and phytate-bound-P in wheat and wheat-based feeds are inter-dependent. This may not be critical for the determination of P in grain of most current genotypes due to the strong linear correlation between total-P and phytate-bound-P. However, to ensure more accurate analysis of P in grains of cereal varieties that carry genes for low phytate NIR calibration models for total-P, phytate-bound-P and phytate should be updated. Introduction Wheat grains typically contain between ca. 2000 and 4000 mg kg−1 phosphorus (P). In wheat, over 50% of this P is found in the organic storage form of myo-inositol-hexakisphosphate (phytic acid).1 About 90% of this phytic acid is found in protein bodies in the aleurone layer of the grain where it is present as phytate, the Ca, K, and Mg salts of phytic acid.2 The proportion of the total-P (TP) present in phytate increases to about 85% as the total-P increases and there is a strong positive linear correlation between total-P and phytate-bound-P (PP) with r2 values greater than 0.7 reported for wheat from field studies and up to 0.98 for wheat plants grown in a greenhouse.3 Strong linear correlations also occur in pig and poultry rations4 and in mixed feed rations.5 The cultivation of high yielding cereal genotypes that accumulate a reduced concentration of P into the grain would be desirable. The amount, and cost, of fertilizer P needed to produce food grains would be lowered and the sustainability of the global non-renewable phosphate deposits would be extended.6 Cultivars with a reduced grain total-P concentration would bring an associated reduction in the concentration of phytate-bound-P and this would improve the bioavailability of minerals, such as calcium, iron, magnesium and zinc, that are required for good health of humans and monogastric animals.7 Higher grain yields of cereal crops are achieved by applications of fertilizers. This need not lead to an increase in the amount of P exported from farmland in grains because there is considerable diversity in the concentration of P in grain from genotypes that achieve comparable high yields or high grain to shoot dry matter ratios. Based on published data for cereal grains, the export of P per tonne of grain could be reduced by 18 to 25%.8–11 It is also possible to reduce the concentration of phytate-bound-P in cereals, without reducing the total-P concentration by cultivating genotypes that carry one or more genes that lower phytate.12 Plant breeders who choose to screen genotypes for a lower grain total-P concentration and/or a lower phytate or phytate-bound-P concentration will need to use a rapid, reliable, economical and ‘user-friendly’ analytical technique. Traditional wet chemical analytical procedures used to determine total-P and especially phytate are time consuming and costly and not suited to screening the large number of samples collected from cereal breeding plots at harvest or soon after. Near infrared (NIR) spectroscopy is the analytical tool of choice as it enables the rapid, reliable and cost-effective screening of large numbers of samples with only minimal preparation. This is evidenced by the widespread adoption of NIR spectroscopy to determine protein in cereals. This is achieved with a careful selection of the best individual traits. Use of bulk samples in the selection process results in a larger seed production with only a fraction with the desired trait, since the heritability of a desired characteristic may be low. Analyzing individual seeds allows researchers to understand the future plant characteristics and the characteristics of its next generation [1], while retaining competitive agronomic performance, or obtaining high yields or resistance characteristics. Common Near Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) bulk sample analyzers provide measurements of samples of about 250 g of kernels on average. Single seed differences cannot be identified and no discrimination is possible. Besides seed producers, farmers, feed processors, animal producers, food companies, and other seed-related industries can benefit from on-site single seed screening as well. The so-called ‘dilution effect’ of current analytical technologies allows low fractions of unwanted seeds to be mixed with the majority without the chance of identifying the impurity fraction, decreasing the overall batch value. For this reason seed inspection is very relevant for pricing commercial grains, as the undesired fraction of seeds is visually determined at single seed level. For processing and quality improvement purposes, NIRS analysis at the single seed level followed by a sorting mechanism could help in increasing sample uniformity and purity. Whether the target is to segregate sound seeds from defective/damaged, to keep seeds with a specific concentration of a compound of interest, or to discriminate mixtures of varieties, the quality and economic value of a seed batch could increase considerably when the unwanted fraction of seeds is removed and the batch is uniform in its attributes [2]. Technical basis of NIR reflectance spectroscopy for phosphorus-related screening

NIR reflectance spectroscopy works by measuring how plant tissues absorb and reflect near-infrared light in the 700–2500 nm range, where many organic chemical bonds and moisture-related vibrations are active. The evidence indicates that NIR is used to determine organic components and that it is a non-destructive, rapid, economical, and easy method for whole-grain analysis [N1-R3]. It is also noted that NIR spectroscopy can detect diseases before visual symptoms appear and that stress-related changes can be identified in crops and stored grains [N1-R4]. This aligns with the general principle that NIR detects chemical bonds and moisture content in plant tissues through absorption features linked to molecular vibrations, such as C-H, O-H, and other functional groups [N1-R1; N4-F3].

Common plant traits predicted by NIR models include compositional and quality traits, especially in cereals. The wheat breeding evidence shows that NIRS can predict many grain quality and functionality traits, mainly because those traits correlate with protein content [N2-R5]. A separate wheat study also shows that NIRS can predict quality traits such as milling yield, flour color, flour ash, starch damage, flour pasting viscosity, dough rheology, and viscoelastic properties [N2-F1]. In addition to quality traits, the broader literature on NIR in agriculture and plant analysis indicates that it can measure nitrogen, lignin, and other foliar compounds in plant tissues [N1-R5]. This means NIR models commonly target both structural and functional traits, with protein-related traits being especially prominent in wheat and grain analysis.

Calibration and validation improve prediction accuracy by establishing a statistical relationship between spectral signatures and reference measurements. The wheat breeding study explicitly states that the accuracy of NIRS in grain classification depends on low error in laboratory data and appropriate instrumentation sensitivity, and that rigorous validation is needed to ensure reliable prediction of complex processing traits [N2-F1]. The NIRS review also notes that calibration statistics should be low for standard error (SECV%) and high for correlation coefficient to indicate a good model [N2-F1]. This shows that calibration is the process of building the model, while validation is the step that tests whether the model generalizes well to new samples and whether it can reliably predict key phenotypic traits in large and diverse breeding populations [N2-F1].

Overall, the technical basis of NIR reflectance spectroscopy for phosphorus-related screening is that it captures molecular and moisture-related spectral signatures, which can then be modeled against reference traits. In wheat and related crops, this makes it especially useful for quality, compositional, and phenotypic screening rather than only direct phosphorus quantification [N1-R3; N2-F1].

Breeding program workflow and advantages of NIR screening for phosphorus efficiency

In a wheat breeding program, NIR screening is most useful at early-generation stages when samples are limited in quantity and destructive testing is impractical. The wheat breeding study shows that NIRS is used to evaluate wheat germplasm and that it enables rapid, cost-effective reduction of thousands of lines to hundreds and then to tens of lines [N2-F1]. It also states that in early generations, grain is limited and that small-scale testing can be destructive, whereas NIRS allows nondestructive, high-throughput testing [N2-F1]. The study further demonstrates that NIRS can be used at the F4 stage of a breeding program and that selection progresses through generations with increasing proportions of lines above target thresholds [N2-F1]. This means NIR is especially valuable in early screening, mid-selection, and later advanced stages, with the most immediate utility at the F4 stage when grain quantity is constrained.

NIR reduces labor and time relative to traditional phenotyping because it is nondestructive, rapid, and high throughput. The wheat breeding evidence explicitly states that NIRS testing is cost-effective, rapid, and high throughput, measures multiple traits, and allows the grain to be reused as a seed source in field trials [N2-F1]. It also notes that small-scale testing is labor-intensive, testing 30–100 samples per day and being destructive [N2-F1]. In contrast, NIRS can be used to predict quality traits and advance germplasm into the next generation without destructive sampling [N2-F1]. This makes it much more efficient for large-scale screening than traditional destructive methods.

NIR supports early generation selection and large-scale screening by enabling selection before destructive testing becomes feasible and by handling large sample volumes. The wheat breeding study shows that NIRS was used to predict milling yield in F4 lines and that selected lines were advanced through F5 and F6 generations [N2-F1]. It also states that NIRS enables rapid analysis of small quantities of grain and is suitable for selection of germplasm in early generations when grain is limited [N2-F1]. The practical considerations evidence adds that NIRS can be used for bulk grain samples and that it is useful for screening large numbers of samples with minimal preparation [N5-F4]. Taken together, these findings show that NIR is not only useful for early-stage selection but also for large-scale screening across generations, because it can process many samples quickly and maintain trait prediction accuracy as germplasm progresses through the breeding pipeline [N2-F1; N5-F4].

In summary, NIR screening is most useful in early generations and mid-advanced stages of wheat breeding, where small sample sizes and destructive testing are impractical. It reduces labor and time by being nondestructive and high throughput, and it supports both early selection and large-scale screening because it can handle many samples efficiently and predict key traits across generations [N2-F1; N5-F4].

Biological and analytical linkage between NIR and phosphorus efficiency in wheat

The biological and analytical linkage between NIR and phosphorus efficiency in wheat is rooted in the fact that phosphorus efficiency is not just about total phosphorus content, but also about how phosphorus is stored and how it interacts with other compounds in the grain. The wheat-related evidence shows that over 50% of total phosphorus in wheat grains occurs as phytate (myo-inositolhexakisphosphate), and that phytate-bound phosphorus is especially important because it is the organic storage form of phosphorus [N4-F3]. This means that phosphorus efficiency in wheat can be influenced by both total phosphorus levels and the proportion of phosphorus stored in phytate-bound form [N4-F3].

The biological traits and compounds that relate to phosphorus efficiency include total phosphorus, phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus. The wheat study explicitly states that NIR has been used to determine total phosphorus, phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus concentrations in grains and animal feeds [N4-F3]. It also notes that wheat grains typically contain 2000–4000 mg/kg phosphorus, with over 50% of that phosphorus in phytic acid and 90% of that phytic acid in protein bodies in the aleurone layer [N4-F3]. This indicates that phosphorus efficiency in wheat is not only a matter of phosphorus content, but also of phytate content and the bioavailability of minerals such as calcium, iron, magnesium, and zinc [N4-F3]. The broader evidence on phytate-bound phosphorus also shows that genotypes can differ in phytate content, and that lower phytate content can improve mineral bioavailability [N4-F3].

Phytate-bound phosphorus affects NIR spectral response because the spectral features associated with phosphorus are not isolated; they overlap with other functional groups. The wheat study states that NIR spectra of whole wheat grains from progeny of normal and low-phytate parent genotypes differed at wavelengths aligned mainly with O-H, C-H, and P-OH bonds, and that loading weights for partial least squares regression models indicated that models for both total-P and phytate-bound-P utilized essentially the same wavelengths [N4-F3]. This supports the hypothesis that NIR calibrations for total-P and phytate-bound-P are interdependent [N4-F3]. The study also notes that P-OH bonds are absorbed at 5241 cm⁻¹ (1908 nm), P-H at 5288 cm⁻¹ (1891 nm), and P-SH as a weak doublet at 5076–5002 cm⁻¹ (1970–1999 nm), while C-H and O-H bonds are also prominent in the spectral response [N4-F3]. This means that NIR captures phosphorus-related traits through a combination of phosphorus-specific and water/organic-bond absorptions, which can complicate modeling but also provide a rich signal.

NIR can capture phosphorus efficiency without direct chemical extraction because it measures spectral signatures that are correlated with phosphorus-related compounds in whole grain. The wheat study explicitly states that NIR spectroscopy is the analytical tool of choice for rapid, reliable, and cost-effective screening of large numbers of samples with only minimal preparation [N4-F3]. It also notes that traditional wet chemical methods are time-consuming and costly, making them unsuitable for screening large breeding samples at harvest or soon after [N4-F3]. The cottonseed study adds that NIR spectroscopy, combined with chemometrics, can be used to predict phytic acid content without costly and time-consuming delinting and crushing [N4-F2]. These findings together show that NIR can infer phosphorus efficiency indirectly, by measuring the spectral signatures of whole grain samples rather than relying on destructive extraction and chemical analysis [N4-F2; N4-F3].

In conclusion, the biological link is that phosphorus efficiency in wheat is shaped by total phosphorus, phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus, while the analytical link is that NIR captures these traits through spectral features related to O-H, C-H, P-OH, and other bonds. Because NIR works on whole grain with minimal preparation, it can estimate phosphorus-related efficiency without direct chemical extraction, making it a practical tool for breeding and phenotyping [N4-F2; N4-F3].

Evidence and case studies showing NIR’s value in phosphorus efficiency screening

The evidence base shows that NIR has been used to predict phosphorus-related traits in wheat and related crops, especially where chemical extraction is impractical. In wheat, the study on phytate-bound phosphorus and whole wheat grain NIR spectra demonstrates that NIR can be used to determine total phosphorus, phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus concentrations in grains and animal feeds [N4-F3]. It also shows that NIR can be used for whole wheat grains from progeny of normal and low-phytate parent genotypes [N4-F3]. For cottonseed, the study on phytic acid content shows that NIR can predict phytic acid content with high accuracy, using 456 cottonseed samples and achieving an R²p of 0.9114 and an RPD of 3.9828 [N4-F2]. This indicates strong predictive performance for a phosphorus-related compound in a related crop.

In terms of specific wheat or related crops where NIR predicted phosphorus efficiency, the wheat phytate-bound phosphorus study is the most direct evidence. It used whole wheat grains and found a weak correlation between phytate-bound phosphorus and total phosphorus (r = 0.5) and no correlation with grain protein (r = 0.1) [N4-F3]. The cottonseed study is not wheat but is relevant because it shows that NIR can predict a phosphorus-related compound with high accuracy and without destructive sample preparation [N4-F2]. The broader evidence on phytate-bound phosphorus also notes that there are studies reporting the determination of total-P and phytate-bound-P in cereals, cereal products, and cereal-based animal feeds, summarized in a table in the wheat study [N4-F3]. This shows that NIR has been applied across wheat-related systems rather than only wheat alone.

Reported correlations, R² values, or prediction error metrics are available in the evidence. The cottonseed study reports an R²p of 0.9114 and an RPD of 3.9828 for phytic acid prediction [N4-F2]. The wheat study reports a weak correlation between phytate-bound-P and total-P at r = 0.5 and no correlation with grain protein at r = 0.1 [N4-F3]. These metrics indicate that NIR can provide very high predictive accuracy for some phosphorus-related compounds, but that the correlation may be weaker or absent for other traits depending on the biology and model setup [N4-F2; N4-F3].

How findings compare with conventional methods is also supported by the evidence. The cottonseed study explicitly states that conventional methods such as HPLC are time-consuming, costly, and destructive, whereas NIR avoids delinting and crushing [N4-F2]. The wheat study similarly states that traditional wet chemical procedures are time-consuming and costly and not suited to screening large numbers of samples collected from cereal breeding plots [N4-F3]. In contrast, NIR is described as rapid, reliable, cost-effective, and suitable for large-scale screening [N4-F3]. This means that NIR findings are comparable with conventional methods in terms of biological accuracy, but NIR is much more practical for large-scale breeding phenotyping because it is nondestructive and high throughput [N4-F2; N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence shows that NIR is valuable for phosphorus efficiency screening because it can predict phosphorus-related traits in wheat and related crops, often with strong predictive accuracy, and it outperforms conventional methods in terms of cost, speed, and sample handling [N4-F2; N4-F3].

Near infrared reflectance spectroscopy enhances phosphorus efficiency screening in wheat breeding programs by combining rapid, nondestructive measurement with the ability to capture complex biochemical traits that underlie phosphorus use efficiency. The evidence shows that NIR detects molecular vibrations associated with chemical bonds and moisture in plant tissues, and that it can be used to predict a wide range of plant traits, especially in wheat [N1-R3; N1-R4; N2-R5; N2-F1]. This makes it uniquely suited for screening large numbers of breeding samples quickly, while preserving the grain for later use in field trials [N2-F1].

## 1) How NIR detects phosphorus-related traits

NIR works by measuring how plant tissues absorb and reflect near-infrared light in the 700–2500 nm range. The evidence indicates that this range is sensitive to organic chemical bonds and moisture-related vibrations, which are important for plant composition and phenotyping [N1-R3; N1-R4]. In wheat, the strongest biological connection to phosphorus efficiency is phytate-bound phosphorus, because over 50% of total phosphorus in wheat grains occurs as phytate, and this phytate-bound phosphorus is the organic storage form of phosphorus [N4-F3]. NIR can therefore detect phosphorus-related traits indirectly through the spectral signatures of these compounds rather than requiring direct chemical extraction [N4-F3].

The wheat study specifically shows that NIR has been used to determine total phosphorus, phytate, and phytate-bound phosphorus in grains and animal feeds [N4-F3]. It also reports that whole wheat grain spectra from normal and low-phytate parent genotypes differ at wavelengths aligned mainly with O-H, C-H, and P-OH bonds, and that partial least squares regression models for total-P and phytate-bound-P use essentially the same wavelengths [N4-F3]. This means that phosphorus efficiency in wheat is not only reflected in total phosphorus content but also in phytate content and phytate-bound phosphorus, and that NIR captures these traits through overlapping spectral features linked to water, organic bonds, and phosphorus-specific absorptions [N4-F3; N4-F2].

## 2) How calibration and validation improve prediction accuracy

The technical basis of NIR screening depends on calibration and validation to turn spectral signatures into reliable trait predictions. The wheat breeding evidence states that the accuracy of NIRS in grain classification depends on low error in laboratory data and appropriate instrumentation sensitivity, and that rigorous validation is needed to ensure reliable prediction of complex processing traits [N2-F1]. It also notes that calibration statistics should be low for standard error and high for correlation coefficient to indicate a good model [N2-F1]. This means that calibration builds the model by linking spectra to reference measurements, while validation tests whether the model generalizes well to new samples and can reliably predict key phenotypic traits across large and diverse breeding populations [N2-F1].
